title: The first family reaches Doire ghlas
summary: A woman, three children and her husband's father, too lame to walk the whole road, reach Ellen Marsh's own gate at Doire ghlas out of the western hills, the first of a trickle that will not stop by the year's end. They say only the town's name, Àth leathan, and no more.

title: The eleven of Muileann àrsaidh
summary: Eleven souls of three farms near Muileann àrsaidh leave together in the night before the ditch-bridge falls, judging a siege at hand and choosing the road north over the ring that is about to close. They reach Doire ghlas and Caol mhòr within the fortnight.

title: Àth leathan's pits given as flooded
summary: A woman of Àth leathan tells Ellen Marsh plainly, in the humans' tongue and then in Dia-thìris, that her town's pits were flooded by the regiments' own order within a day of the fighting's end, so that nothing is left there for her household to return to.

title: Hugh Ferris's wage-ledger
summary: An old hewer of Àth leathan, forty years at the coal and ten more keeper of the pit-shed's tallies, carries away under his coat the ledger of wages owed him rather than any clothing or food, and gives it to Ellen Marsh to keep beside her own books.

title: The Moot's granaries opened at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas
summary: Martha Greaves opens the granaries kept full since the year before on the wool mills' own takings, the nine votes of the winter past read by Peter Hale as a promise already made and now only kept. The council sends nothing north and forbids nothing.

title: Martha Greaves writes to the Library
summary: Martha Greaves writes to Sìleas nic Rath at Muileann chaol, not to ask anything of the Library but to set down, outside her own kitchen table, that the Moot has fed the west's hungry while the council has sent nothing north and forbidden nothing.

title: Thomas Rook's register begun
summary: Thomas Rook rules a plain ledger into columns, name, town of origin, family and taken in, and keeps it from the first week of the families' coming. By the end of an Cèitean he counts three hundred and forty souls taken in at Caol mhòr and Doire ghlas together.

title: William Reid questions the promise's floor
summary: At a sitting called out of the calendar, the eastern delegate William Reid asks the room whether it has considered that a promise to feed the west's people indefinitely was made without knowing how long the feeding would be needed. Martha Greaves answers that the not knowing excuses nothing.

title: Agnes Pike's school given over
summary: The school Agnes Pike built at Doire ghlas thirty years before is given over, in the last week of an Cèitean, to families with no roof of their own; by midsummer near sixty souls sleep on its benches, pushed together in twos and threes with a blanket over the gap.

title: Ellen Marsh's twelfth book begun
summary: Ellen Marsh begins, without quite deciding to begin it, a twelfth book, kept in Dia-thìris as her eleven before it, of what the war's families tell her in the school's hall of an evening: not a life's telling saved up, but the sharp particular things a mind cannot help keeping.

title: The families name the war-book
summary: The families sheltered under Agnes Pike's roof come, within the first month, to call Ellen Marsh's new book the war-book among themselves, and bring things to it the way a thing is brought to be weighed, whether or not she ever asked them for a telling.

title: Hugh Ferris's account of the pit-shed
summary: The old hewer of Àth leathan gives Ellen Marsh, for the war-book, an exact accounting of the pit-shed where Ruth Calder once read out the agreement of the five towns, believing it flooded or fallen, and wishing it set down once more before it goes under.

title: A child gives Ruth Calder's name
summary: A girl of the Muileann àrsaidh eleven asks Ellen Marsh to set Ruth Calder's name in the war-book, though she has, by her own word, nothing true to give beside it: only what her mother says of a name dropped from every list the kingdom keeps since the spring.

title: Nell Forbes's dresser
summary: A woman of Àth leathan sheltering at Doire ghlas tells Ellen Marsh that she thinks more often of the kitchen dresser she left with the plates on it than of the house itself.

title: A harbour boy's word on beggaring
summary: A harbourmaster's boy of Caol mhòr tells the speaker of the Moot, repeating his father, that the Moot will beggar itself feeding the western hills and serve the council right.

title: Seed-corn sent west from Caol mhòr
summary: The Moot sends seed-corn from the stores at Caol mhòr to the farms of the western hills that fed the column's families, entered in the roll as a loan with no term.

title: Meal from Cnoc ghorm for Doire ghlas
summary: The Tuathaich of Cnoc ghorm send three carts of meal down to Doire ghlas for the western families in Agnes Pike's school, the carters asking no receipt.

title: Doire shean's market-clerk counts the tithe
summary: At Doire shean the market-clerk, who keeps the new count and the old side by side, keeps a third column now for the tithe paid at the harbour pump.
